summary: We straved towards a renovation and rethink of the classroom games paradigm. This newer generations of children lack the development opportunities for their psychomotor skills. JEZERO comes as a response in the present digital direction with a positive glance at our past student (and young) versions.
details: Project Jezero – Learning to live on Mars. What it does: Project Jezero is a hands-on game that teaches children how a Mars base stays alive. The base is a physical tabletop model. Four 3D-printed modules stand on a hexagonal Martian floor, and each one has its own touchscreen: Power, Water, Mine and Greenhouse. Each screen has a mascot, such as a battery, a water drop, a rock or a plant. A laptop or phone shows a 3D digital twin of the same base, where the colony grows, colonists walk around and the player chooses what to build next. The game starts with a guided tutorial. A friendly on-board computer asks the child to tap the rock to mine minerals and tap the battery to get energy, until they can build their first solar panels. From then on the base starts producing resources on its own. The child expands it with habitats, oxygen generators, water recycling, crops, wind turbines and a reactor, and eventually builds a rocket to found a new colony or return to Earth. The physical modules matter because problems happen in the real world. A dust storm cuts solar power by 80%. When the battery runs out, the base shuts systems down in order: mine, then food, then water, and oxygen last. The child has to walk to the Power module and rub the dirty panels on the screen to bring production back. Each breakdown has its own gesture. You draw circles to recharge an over-discharged battery, tap to break rocks after a cave-in, swipe to clean contaminated water, hold to water a wilted plant, and tap to crack frozen pipes. What children learn: the systems of a base depend on each other. Without energy there is no oxygen. Without water there is no food and no oxygen. Dust, night and radiation all limit what you can do. Children learn this by doing, not by reading. They see the mine stop, they understand why, and they fix it with their own hands. NASA data: the day and night cycle uses a real solar elevation profile from the NASA/JPL Horizons API, sped up so that one sol takes 10 minutes. Panels stop at night and the battery has to cover the gap. Dust storms are based on NASA/JPL InSight data, whose power output fell from about 5,000 Wh to about 500 Wh per sol as dust covered its panels. The solar storm event is inspired by Curiosity's observations of the May 2024 solar storm (NASA/JPL-Caltech, PIA26302). Children choose between taking shelter, raising a shield that costs battery, or taking the risk, and a dosimeter shows the radiation dose each choice produces. We keep a clear line between real data and simplified game rules, such as timings and percentages, and we say so in the game and the documentation. Benefits and intended impact: it turns abstract ideas like life support, energy balance and resource dependency into something children can touch, see and fix. Children cannot lose. Shortages slow the base down but never kill colonists. Manual help always lets them recover, so they learn from mistakes without frustration. It works for groups: several children can play at once, each looking after a module, which encourages teamwork and talking things through. It is cheap and easy to copy for schools, museums and science fairs: about €15 ESP32 boards, printed cases with no screws, and free software. Anyone can open the game on their phone by scanning a QR code. We tested an early prototype with children and used what we saw to adjust the gestures and the pacing. Tools, languages, hardware and software: for hardware, 4 ESP32-2432S028 "Cheap Yellow Display" boards with 2.8" touchscreens, AA battery packs, and cases, floor tiles and a command center designed by us and printed on a Bambu Lab P1S. We also made two-color astronaut keychains as a takeaway. The firmware is written in C++ with the Arduino framework and PlatformIO, including custom scenes, animated mascots, touch gestures and touch calibration. The game server uses Python with FastAPI and WebSockets. Python is the only authority for game rules: economy, power balance, events, population and the save system. It includes a simulator so we can test without hardware. The digital twin uses JavaScript with three.js (WebGPU) and Vite, with four quality levels and a benchmark so it runs on ordinary laptops. It is available in Spanish and English. We also used the NASA/JPL Horizons API, a Cloudflare tunnel with a QR code to play from any device, Playwright for automated tests, and Python scripts that generate our videos and sound effects. Our two-person team also worked with AI coding agents (Claude Code and Codex), which coordinated through GitHub issues. How it is creative: most space education games live entirely on a screen. Ours puts the base on the table. The digital twin and the physical model always mirror each other: when you fix the panels with your finger, the 3D base comes back to life. Each repair gesture copies the real action, like rubbing off dust or watering a plant. The cute mascots grow and evolve as you upgrade them, which makes children care about each system. The game follows the proven loop of incremental games: tap, automate, expand, and found a new colony. We tuned it so there is always a clear next goal and something new on screen. Factors we considered: for age and accessibility, short texts, one instruction at a time, big touch targets, no reading-heavy menus on the small screens, and no way to fail permanently. For scientific honesty, real NASA data where it exists, and simplifications that are clearly labeled. For cost and reproducibility, cheap off-the-shelf boards, printable parts and open source code. For reliability in live demos, touches are retried and never counted twice, there are save files, and the game can be tested without the boards. For engagement, we studied what makes incremental games fun or boring and checked every new mechanic against that list.
